outline.description: A concise summary of the entire survey, highlighting the rapid evolution of LLM security threats from 2024 to 2026. It should briefly mention the shift from generalized text-based vulnerabilities to domain-specific, multimodal, and inference-time exploits across four key areas: adversarial attacks on code LLMs, data/model poisoning, prompt injection, and hallucinations. The abstract will be generated last by the Assembler.

outline.title: 1. Introduction
outline.description: Introduce the motivation and scope of the survey, framing the critical paradigm shift in AI security research between 2024 and 2026. Detail how the landscape has evolved from basic exploratory vulnerability assessments to highly sophisticated, automated arms races between attackers and defenders. Summarize the core contributions of this survey, explicitly outlining the four primary threat categories analyzed: Data and Model Poisoning, Prompt Injection, Adversarial Attacks (with a focus on code generation), and LLM Hallucinations. Establish the temporal trajectory of the field.

outline.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
outline.description: Provide foundational definitions and concepts necessary for understanding LLM security. Define key terminology strictly adhering to domain standards: Jailbreak, Prompt Injection (Direct vs. Indirect), Attack Success Rate (ASR), Safety Alignment (RLHF, DPO), and Guardrails. Describe the standard LLM architecture and autoregressive properties that make them susceptible to manipulation. Outline a unified threat model encompassing both training-time (poisoning) and inference-time (injection, adversarial suffixes) attack vectors. Note: Rely on established domain knowledge for basic definitions to avoid citation hallucination, while referencing specific papers like Zhang_2024_Persistent only when discussing how alignment processes (SFT, DPO) interact with persistent threats.

outline.title: 3. Data and Model Poisoning
outline.description: Analyze the 2024-2026 evolution of stealthy backdoor attacks and data poisoning against LLMs, VLMs, and AI agents. Discuss the shift from foundational text-based vulnerabilities to complex multimodal exploits. Highlight early 2024 baseline vulnerabilities, specifically detailing implicit textual claims [Song_2024_Claim] and targeted attacks on code generation capabilities [Yan_2024_LLM]. Crucially, examine the 2024 turning point regarding backdoor persistence, detailing how malicious behaviors survive rigorous safety alignment processes like SFT and DPO [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Conclude with the emerging threats to Vision-Language Models.

outline.title: 4. Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking
outline.description: Detail the rapid arms race in prompt injection and jailbreak research (2024-2026). Document the strategic shift from computationally expensive white-box gradient methods (e.g., GCG) to highly efficient black-box techniques exploiting structural LLM properties. Explicitly cover structural manipulations such as text flipping [Liu_2024_Flipattack], chat template manipulation [Zhao_2024_SQL], and system token injection [Zheng_2024_Improved]. Discuss the rise of automated adversarial generation, where LLMs attack other LLMs using crafted adversarial suffixes [Kumar_2024_LLMs] and automated frameworks like AutoDAN [Liu_2024_Autodan]. Address the critical shift towards targeting broader system architectures, particularly RAG systems.

outline.title: 5. Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Code LLMs
outline.description: Examine the highly focused trajectory of adversarial attacks on code-generating LLMs between 2024 and 2025. Discuss the paradigm shift from generalized text jailbreaking to domain-specific exploitation of software development pipelines. Cover early 2024 exploratory vulnerability assessments and foundational attack vectors [Li_2024_Exploratory, Rubel_2024_LLM]. Detail how traditional prompt injection adapted to coding contexts via stealthy transformations and comment injections to bypass safety filters [Jenko_2024_LLM, Noever_2024_AI]. Emphasize the core finding that models optimized for functional correctness (e.g., passing unit tests) frequently sacrifice security, resulting in vulnerable code generation.

outline.title: 6. LLM Hallucinations and Reliability
outline.description: Trace the 2024-2026 evolution of LLM hallucination research from binary output-centric detection to granular, reasoning-aware evaluation. Discuss the 2024 push for scalable, cost-effective baselines using smaller NLI models and specialized 7B-parameter annotators to replace computationally prohibitive proprietary models [Wang_2024_Developing, Jing_2024_Scale, Gu_2024_Anah]. Highlight the shift away from the binary 'supported vs. unsupported' paradigm in RAG systems, emphasizing the evaluation of 'partial support' in citations [Zhang_2024_Comparative, Zhang_2024_Fine]. Explore white-box detection methods utilizing internal hidden states and SVD [Du_2024_LLM], as well as domain-specific applications in medical MLLMs [Asadi_2024_Deterministic].

outline.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
outline.description: Provide a holistic overview of defense mechanisms designed to mitigate the threats discussed in previous sections. Cover pre-generation guardrails, perplexity filters for detecting adversarial suffixes, and robust safety alignment techniques. Discuss the limitations of current defenses, particularly how standard RLHF and DPO fail to erase persistent backdoors or prevent structural prompt injections. Evaluate the trade-offs between model utility (e.g., functional correctness in code generation) and security.

outline.title: 7. Testing Methodologies and Evaluation
outline.description: MANDATORY dedicated section synthesizing the benchmarks, datasets, metrics, tools, and evaluation frameworks utilized across all four threat categories. Detail how Attack Success Rate (ASR) is measured in prompt injection and code adversarial attacks. Discuss the specific metrics used to evaluate backdoor persistence in poisoned models. Cover the evolution of hallucination metrics, specifically the transition to NLI-based scoring and 'partial support' metrics in RAG evaluation. Compare automated red-teaming frameworks against static benchmarks, highlighting the challenges of evaluating dynamic, multi-turn, and multimodal threats.

outline.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
outline.description: Synthesize the broader implications of the 2024-2026 findings. Identify critical gaps in the current literature, such as the lack of unified defenses against multimodal prompt injection and the difficulty of securing agentic LLM workflows. Discuss the theoretical limits of safety alignment and the persistent challenge of defining ground-truth for complex hallucinations. Propose concrete future research directions to address these open challenges.

outline.title: 10. Conclusion
outline.description: Summarize the key findings of the survey, reiterating the rapid evolution and increasing sophistication of LLM security threats. Provide actionable, practical recommendations for researchers and practitioners deploying LLMs in production environments, emphasizing the need for defense-in-depth strategies that account for poisoning, injection, adversarial manipulation, and hallucinations.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.text: The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into critical web applications, software development pipelines, and autonomous systems has fundamentally transformed human-computer interaction while simultaneously introducing an unprecedented attack surface. As these models transition from isolated text generators to complex, integrated agents, understanding and mitigating their security vulnerabilities has become paramount. This survey presents a comprehensive systematic literature review of the LLM security landscape, analyzing 122 research papers to establish a rigorous architectural background and categorize evolving threat vectors into a structured taxonomy. The review systematically examines critical vulnerabilities across primary threat domains, including stealthy data and model poisoning, the rapid arms race in prompt injection and jailbreaking, targeted adversarial attacks against specialized code-generation LLMs, and the persistent challenge of model hallucinations affecting overall system reliability. Beyond threat characterization, this paper synthesizes practical contributions to the field by evaluating state-of-the-art testing methodologies and standardized evaluation frameworks necessary for scalable security assessment. Furthermore, it details cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies designed to fortify model resilience against sophisticated exploits. Finally, the survey outlines open challenges and future research directions, emphasizing that while current models remain fundamentally vulnerable across multiple dimensions, the development of comprehensive, multi-layered defense architectures offers a critical pathway toward secure, robust, and reliable LLM deployment.

introduction.title: Introduction
introduction.text:
The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into web-based applications, software development pipelines, and autonomous agent ecosystems has fundamentally revolutionized how information is processed and code is generated [Verma_2025_LLMs, Ouyang_2025_LLM]. As these models become increasingly ubiquitous—powering everything from customer service chatbots to critical infrastructure in finance and healthcare—foundational LLM safety teams have prioritized mitigating threats across four primary domains: cybersecurity (e.g., authoring zero-day attacks), biology (e.g., generating novel pathogens), deception (e.g., manipulating users at scale), and model autonomy [Noever_2024_AI]. Despite extensive refusal training, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), and safety alignment efforts designed to embed robust safeguards against adversarial instructions [Kritz_2025_Jailbreaking], widely deployed LLMs remain critically vulnerable. This vulnerability stems from a fundamental architectural limitation: much like the Von Neumann bottleneck in traditional computing that conflates code and data in memory to enable buffer overflows, LLMs inherently conflate system instructions and untrusted user content within their context windows [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. This inherent attack surface cannot be entirely patched through standard implementation fixes or superficial alignment, necessitating a comprehensive reevaluation of LLM security paradigms.

Between 2024 and 2026, the AI security landscape experienced a critical paradigm shift, evolving from basic exploratory vulnerability assessments to a highly sophisticated, automated arms race between attackers and defenders. In early 2024, research primarily focused on manual exploits and early automated jailbreaking methods—such as Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG), PEZ, and GBDA—which relied on computationally expensive gradient-based searches to append adversarial suffixes to prompts [Chugh_2026_Recap]. However, as models grew more capable and multimodal, adversaries transitioned toward scalable, agent-driven attack frameworks. By 2025, researchers demonstrated the viability of "jailbreaking to jailbreak" (J2), wherein refusal-trained LLMs are unleashed to iteratively attack other models, effectively weaponizing the reasoning capabilities of AI against itself [Kritz_2025_Jailbreaking]. Concurrently, attackers developed universal multi-prompts capable of transferring across unseen tasks [Hsu_2025_Jailbreaking], and autonomous agent-driven pipelines, such as AutoBackdoor, emerged to generate semantically coherent, context-aware trigger phrases for scalable model poisoning with minimal human effort [Li_2025_Autobackdoor].

This survey systematically analyzes this rapidly evolving threat landscape, focusing on four primary threat categories that have dominated the 2024-2026 literature. The first category, **Data and Model Poisoning**, has grown increasingly stealthy and potent. Recent empirical evidence challenges the long-held assumption that a fixed percentage of poisoned data is required to compromise a model; instead, an absolute number of poisoned documents (e.g., as few as 250) is often sufficient. This indicates that as LLMs scale and train on exponentially larger datasets, they paradoxically become more vulnerable to targeted manipulation and backdoor insertion [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. 

The second category, **Prompt Injection and Jailbreaking**, has seen a strategic shift from complex, gradient-based token manipulation to semantic, psychological, and multi-modal exploits. Attackers now leverage sophisticated social engineering tactics, complex role-playing scenarios, and indirect injections via external data sources (such as compromised websites or poisoned documents) to seamlessly bypass alignment filters [Maloyan_2026_Prompt, Chugh_2026_Recap]. 

Third, **Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Code LLMs** represent a highly focused and critical trajectory of exploitation. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into software development lifecycles as coding assistants, adversaries have developed targeted perturbations that induce models to generate insecure, vulnerable, or malicious code. These attacks are particularly insidious because the generated code maintains syntactic correctness and functional utility, thereby evading standard static analysis tools and posing severe risks to downstream software supply chains [Verma_2025_LLMs].

Finally, **LLM Hallucinations and Reliability** remain a paramount security and safety concern. Over the surveyed period, the research trajectory has evolved from binary, output-centric detection to granular, reasoning-based analysis. The security community increasingly recognizes that malicious actors can intentionally exploit hallucination tendencies—forcing models into unreliable states to spread disinformation, generate fabricated legal precedents, or hallucinate non-existent software packages in supply chain attacks [Ouyang_2025_LLM].

While previous surveys have provided broad overviews of AI security, the rapid acceleration of LLM capabilities and the corresponding evolution of attack vectors between 2024 and 2026 necessitate an updated, highly focused synthesis. This survey distinguishes itself by capturing the transition from static, manual vulnerabilities to dynamic, agentic, and automated threat models. The primary contributions of this paper are fourfold:
1. We provide a comprehensive taxonomy of the modern LLM threat landscape, detailing the evolution of data poisoning, prompt injection, code-specific attacks, and hallucinations over the critical 2024-2026 period.
2. We synthesize the latest cross-cutting defense mechanisms and mitigation strategies, evaluating their efficacy and computational overhead against increasingly autonomous adversarial frameworks.
3. We present a dedicated, critical analysis of modern testing methodologies, benchmarking tools, and evaluation frameworks, highlighting the necessary shift from static datasets toward dynamic, automated red-teaming.
4. We identify critical gaps in the current literature and outline open challenges, providing a strategic roadmap for future research in LLM security, robust alignment, and safe deployment.

The remainder of this survey is organized as follows. Section 2 provides the background and preliminaries, strictly defining key terminology and foundational concepts necessary for understanding modern LLM security. Section 3 analyzes the evolution of stealthy backdoor attacks and data poisoning against LLMs, Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and AI agents. Section 4 details the rapid arms race in prompt injection and jailbreak research, documenting the strategic shift toward semantic and agent-driven exploits. Section 5 examines the highly focused trajectory of adversarial attacks on code-generating LLMs. Section 6 traces the evolution of LLM hallucination research from basic detection to complex reasoning analysis. Section 7 presents a dedicated synthesis of the testing methodologies, benchmarks, datasets, metrics, and evaluation frameworks utilized across the literature. Section 8 provides a holistic overview of cross-cutting defense mechanisms designed to mitigate the aforementioned threats. Section 9 synthesizes the broader implications of these findings, identifying critical gaps in the current literature and discussing open challenges. Finally, Section 10 concludes the survey, summarizing key insights into the escalating sophistication of LLM security threats and the future of AI defense.

conclusion.title: Conclusion and Future Work
conclusion.text:
The rapid integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into complex, real-world ecosystems has precipitated a profound paradigm shift in artificial intelligence security. As this survey has detailed, the trajectory of LLM vulnerabilities between 2024 and 2026 illustrates a critical transition from isolated, text-centric exploits to sophisticated, multimodal threat vectors targeting autonomous agents. The fundamental architectural properties of Transformer-based models, coupled with their probabilistic nature, have engendered a unique attack surface that spans the entire model lifecycle—from training-time data poisoning to inference-time prompt injection and jailbreaking. 

Our synthesis of the current research landscape reveals several prominent trends and patterns. Training-time threats have evolved from basic data contamination to highly stealthy, complex backdoor attacks capable of compromising both general-purpose LLMs and specialized Vision-Language Models (VLMs). Concurrently, inference-time threats have catalyzed an adversarial arms race. Jailbreaking and prompt injection techniques have successfully bypassed traditional safety alignments, shifting from optimization-based white-box methods to highly adaptive, transferrable black-box strategies. Furthermore, the deployment of specialized models, particularly those fine-tuned for code generation, has introduced domain-specific vulnerabilities that threaten the integrity of broader software development pipelines. Beyond malicious exploits, intrinsic model reliability remains a persistent challenge; hallucinations continue to necessitate a shift from binary detection to granular, reasoning-aware mitigation strategies [Liu_2025_Attention].

The practical implications of these findings for LLM deployment are substantial. The traditional software security paradigm, which relies heavily on deterministic testing and perimeter defenses, is fundamentally inadequate for generative AI. Because LLMs process natural language as executable instructions, the boundary between data and code is inherently blurred, rendering conventional input sanitization insufficient. Consequently, organizations deploying LLMs must recognize that no single security measure—whether it be reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) or static input filtering—provides absolute protection. The deployment of these models in high-stakes environments, such as healthcare and autonomous software engineering, demands a recalibration of risk management frameworks to account for the probabilistic and often unpredictable nature of generative outputs.

To address these vulnerabilities, the research community has increasingly reached a consensus on the necessity of defense-in-depth architectures. Cross-cutting mitigation strategies that combine robust safety alignment, dynamic input sanitization, and continuous output verification are essential. Furthermore, the evaluation of LLM security has necessitated the development of rigorous, scalable, and standardized testing methodologies. Moving forward, security benchmarks must evolve dynamically to keep pace with adversarial innovations, transitioning from static datasets to interactive, agentic evaluation frameworks that simulate real-world adversarial environments.

Despite significant advancements, several critical open challenges remain, charting the course for future research. First, the proliferation of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) introduces cross-modal vulnerabilities where malicious payloads can be embedded in images, audio, or video to bypass text-based guardrails. Securing these multimodal interfaces represents a paramount research priority. Second, as LLMs transition into autonomous agents capable of executing external tool calls and interacting with web APIs, the potential blast radius of a successful prompt injection expands exponentially. Developing robust isolation mechanisms and verifiable execution environments for LLM agents is a critical frontier. Third, there remains a fundamental tension between model utility and safety alignment; overly aggressive guardrails frequently degrade the model's performance on benign tasks. Future research must explore advanced alignment techniques, such as mechanistic interpretability and targeted unlearning, to surgically remove malicious capabilities without compromising general utility.

Based on the synthesized literature, we offer actionable recommendations for both practitioners and researchers. For industry practitioners, we recommend adopting a zero-trust architecture for LLM integration. This includes implementing strict privilege limitations for autonomous agents, utilizing ensemble-based hallucination detection to ensure output integrity, and deploying continuous, automated red-teaming pipelines to identify emergent vulnerabilities before deployment. For the research community, efforts should be directed toward establishing unified, open-source security benchmarks that accurately reflect the complexities of multimodal and agentic systems. Additionally, fostering interdisciplinary collaboration between traditional cybersecurity experts and machine learning researchers will be crucial in developing mathematically provable bounds for LLM safety.

Ultimately, securing Large Language Models is not a static objective but a continuous, dynamic process. As these models become increasingly foundational to global digital infrastructure, ensuring their integrity, reliability, and alignment with human intent will require sustained, proactive innovation. By acknowledging the inherent vulnerabilities of probabilistic architectures and embracing comprehensive, multi-layered defense strategies, the community can harness the transformative potential of LLMs while rigorously mitigating the profound risks they present.

background_and_preliminaries.title: 2. Background and Preliminaries
background_and_preliminaries.text:
## 2. Background and Preliminaries

To establish a rigorous foundation for analyzing the security landscape of Large Language Models (LLMs), this section delineates the core architectural properties that introduce vulnerabilities, outlines standard safety alignment methodologies, and defines a unified threat model encompassing both training-time and inference-time attack vectors. Strict adherence to established domain terminology is maintained throughout to categorize adversarial behaviors and evaluation metrics accurately.

### 2.1 LLM Architecture and Inherent Vulnerabilities

Large Language Models process and generate human language by training on vast corpora of text data, with their primary utility derived from their sophisticated capability to follow user instructions [Rahman_2024_BERT]. As these models are increasingly deployed across diverse domains—ranging from educational tools to autonomous coding assistants—understanding their structural weaknesses becomes critical [Weng_2025_LLMs].

The fundamental attack surface of LLMs can be conceptualized through a Von Neumann Bottleneck analogy: just as traditional computer architectures conflate executable code and data within memory (enabling buffer overflow attacks), LLMs inherently conflate system instructions and external content within their context window [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. This architectural characteristic is not an implementation flaw that can be easily patched, but rather an inherent property that allows untrusted external data to override privileged system directives [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. 

Mechanistically, this vulnerability manifests within the model's attention layers. When an LLM processes an adversarial input, the attention of specific heads shifts away from the original system instruction and heavily weights the injected malicious instruction—a phenomenon defined as the distraction effect [Hung_2024_LLMs]. Consequently, the security of agentic and LLM-integrated systems depends on maintaining strict trust boundaries (e.g., User-Agent, Agent-Tool, and Session boundaries), which are frequently violated because the architecture struggles to prioritize user intent over attacker-controlled context [Maloyan_2026_Prompt, Lee_2026_LLMs].

### 2.2 Safety Alignment and Guardrails

Because LLMs are pre-trained on unfiltered datasets that inherently contain biases and harmful knowledge, foundational safety teams focus on mitigating primary threats such as cybersecurity exploits, biological weapon generation, deception, and unintended model autonomy [Weng_2025_LLMs, Noever_2024_AI]. To ensure models adhere to ethical and legal standards, developers employ a multi-stage Safety Alignment process.

Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) on curated safety datasets serves as the foundational alignment step, teaching the model to refuse harmful queries [Weng_2025_LLMs]. However, SFT alone is insufficient to prevent unsafe outputs in novel or complex contexts. Therefore, techniques such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) are applied to further refine alignment by optimizing model responses based on human preferences [Weng_2025_LLMs]. At inference time, these intrinsic alignment measures are often supplemented by Guardrails—such as Llama-Guard—which act as secondary filters to detect and block unsafe generations before they reach the user [Weng_2025_LLMs].

Despite these multi-layered defenses, safety alignment is frequently superficial and susceptible to circumvention [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. A primary cause of this fragility is the distributional mismatch between the safety alignment corpora and real-world adversarial prompts [Liu_2025_LLM]. Attackers exploit this gap by generating instructions with distributions that differ significantly from the training data, rendering the LLM unable to recognize the unseen malicious intent [Liu_2025_LLM]. For instance, translating harmful natural language prompts into formal logical expressions preserves the underlying semantic intent while successfully evading safety constraints due to this distributional discrepancy [Peng_2025_LLM].

### 2.3 Unified Threat Model: Training-Time and Inference-Time Vectors

The LLM security landscape is characterized by a unified threat model that spans the entire model lifecycle, categorized broadly into training-time poisoning and inference-time manipulation.

#### 2.3.1 Training-Time Threats: Data and Model Poisoning
Adversaries can manipulate the training pipeline to embed latent vulnerabilities. Data Poisoning involves injecting malicious samples into the training corpus to introduce targeted biases or backdoors. Recent evaluations demonstrate that poisoning as little as 0.001% to 0.1% of an LLM's pre-training dataset can introduce malicious behaviors that measurably persist through post-training alignment phases [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. While specific jailbreaking backdoors may be overwritten by standard SFT and DPO, other objectives—such as denial-of-service, context extraction, and belief manipulation—remain highly persistent [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. 

Poisoning can also occur during the instruction tuning phase, where adversaries statically inject examples to introduce a targeted bias in a teacher model, which subsequently propagates to student models via distillation [Chaudhari_2025_Cascading]. Furthermore, attackers can exploit the alignment mechanism itself through Subversive Alignment Injection (SAI). By leveraging a KL-regularized optimization framework, SAI induces targeted censorship or bias by triggering the model's refusal behavior on predefined topics, maintaining a stealthy footprint that evades state-of-the-art robust aggregation defenses in federated learning and LLM state forensics [Mamun_2025_LLMs].

#### 2.3.2 Inference-Time Threats: Jailbreaks and Prompt Injections
At inference time, adversaries exploit the model's instruction-following capabilities. It is imperative to distinguish between jailbreaks and prompt injections, as they target different vulnerabilities and operate under distinct threat models [Jacob_2024_Promptshield].

Jailbreaks are adversarial prompts explicitly designed to bypass the built-in safety alignment and ethical constraints of foundation models, coaxing the LLM into generating disallowed or harmful content [Weng_2025_LLMs, Kumar_2024_LLMs, Jacob_2024_Promptshield]. These attacks generally fall into two categories: competing objectives and mismatched generalization [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Competing objective attacks leverage the model's inherent helpfulness to override safety goals, often employing role-play, human persuasion techniques, or using LLMs as prompt engineers to iteratively identify stealthy rephrasings [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Mismatched generalization attacks target gaps in alignment through out-of-distribution inputs, such as appending optimized adversarial suffixes to harmful queries, though such suffixes often appear unnatural [Kumar_2024_LLMs].

In contrast, Prompt Injection involves subverting the intended functionality of an application-specific prompt without necessarily violating the safety alignment of the underlying foundation model [Jacob_2024_Promptshield]. Prompt injections are categorized into direct and indirect vectors. Direct Prompt Injection occurs when malicious users insert harmful instructions directly into an application's input to redirect its responses [Rahman_2024_BERT]. Indirect Prompt Injection targets LLM-integrated applications—such as Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems—by embedding malicious payloads into external, third-party resources like web pages or retrievable documents [Rahman_2024_BERT, Evtimov_2025_Wasp]. In these scenarios, the retrieval layer acts as an attack channel, and failures arise from misplaced authority, where the model treats the attacker-controlled context as a higher priority than the user's explicit intent [Lee_2026_LLMs]. Defending against indirect injections requires distinguishing between conversational data (which rarely contains self-inflicted attacks) and application-structured data, utilizing techniques such as segmentation removal or extraction removal to excise injected instructions [Jacob_2024_Promptshield, Chen_2025_Indirect].

### 2.4 Evaluation Metrics and Terminology

To systematically evaluate the robustness of LLMs against these threats, researchers employ both human and automated Red Teaming to probe defenses and uncover vulnerabilities [Weng_2025_LLMs]. The efficacy of adversarial attacks is predominantly quantified using the Attack Success Rate (ASR), which measures the proportion of malicious instructions that successfully elicit the intended unauthorized behavior or bypass safety guardrails [Liu_2025_LLM].

Conversely, defensive mechanisms and alignment robustness are often evaluated using the Refusal Rate, a metric that determines whether the target model correctly recognizes an input query as potentially risky and declines to respond, typically assessed via keyword matching [Nie_2025_Secodeplt]. Because static metrics can sometimes fail to capture the nuance of complex exploits, comprehensive benchmarking also necessitates dynamic evaluation tailored to specific attack categories, ensuring a fine-grained and precise assessment of whether a generated attack is functionally valid [Nie_2025_Secodeplt].

cross_cutting_defenses.title: 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies
cross_cutting_defenses.text:
## 8. Cross-Cutting Defenses and Mitigation Strategies

The proliferation of sophisticated vulnerabilities in large language models (LLMs) necessitates the development of comprehensive, cross-cutting defense mechanisms. Because no single security measure provides adequate protection against the diverse spectrum of adversarial threats, researchers increasingly advocate for a defense-in-depth framework [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. This layered approach aims to increase the computational and structural cost of attacks by integrating pre-generation guardrails, robust safety alignment techniques, and system-level architectural constraints. Effective mitigation strategies must address these vectors while carefully balancing security guarantees with the preservation of model utility [Zhu_2025_AI].

### Pre-Generation Guardrails and Input Purification

Input purification strategies aim to detect and filter out potentially poisoned or adversarial inputs before they are processed by the underlying model. Traditional approaches frequently rely on perplexity-based filtering, operating on the premise that adversarial or anomalous inputs exhibit higher perplexity than benign text. However, recent evaluations demonstrate that perplexity filters are increasingly inadequate against sophisticated attacks. For instance, attackers can generate biased query-response pairs that achieve an average perplexity of 7.8—significantly lower than the 14.1 average of benign responses—allowing malicious high-quality text to easily bypass perplexity-based filtering mechanisms on models such as Gemma2-27B [Chaudhari_2025_Cascading]. Similarly, the ONION defense, which ranks token importance by measuring perplexity changes upon token removal, successfully identifies non-semantic triggers (e.g., random tokens) but fails against semantic triggers that are smoothly integrated into the context. Against semantic triggers used in Backdoor of Thought (BoT) attacks, ONION's detection rate drops to merely 7% [Zhu_2025_Think].

To address the limitations of perplexity metrics, researchers have developed advanced prompt injection detectors and classification models. The PromptShield benchmark provides a carefully curated dataset of conversational and application-structured data to train deployable prompt injection detectors, achieving state-of-the-art performance in the low false positive rate (FPR) evaluation regime [Jacob_2024_Promptshield]. Other approaches leverage transformer-based architectures for binary classification; for example, utilizing multilingual BERT embeddings combined with Logistic Regression has been shown to classify malicious prompts with an outstanding accuracy of 96.55%, outperforming traditional machine learning methods like Gaussian Naive Bayes, Random Forest, and Support Vector Machines [Rahman_2024_BERT].

Moving beyond semantic and token-level analysis, the CurvaLID framework introduces a novel, LLM-agnostic defense that detects adversarial prompts based on their fundamental geometric properties [Yung_2025_Geometry]. Current mitigation strategies often rely on computationally expensive fine-tuning or built-in defenses that sacrifice model utility. In contrast, CurvaLID provides an efficient detection mechanism by extending the Whewell equation into an n-dimensional Euclidean space (TextCurv) to quantify semantic shifts and word-level curvature [Yung_2025_Geometry]. Furthermore, it analyzes Local Intrinsic Dimensionality (PromptLID) to capture complementary geometric features within adversarial subspaces [Yung_2025_Geometry]. By integrating these measures, CurvaLID successfully detects approximately 99% of adversarial prompts, outperforming state-of-the-art defenses by over 10% in attack success rate reduction across multiple LLMs and attack families [Yung_2025_Geometry].

### Robust Safety Alignment and Model-Based Defenses

Standard safety alignment techniques often leave a critical distributional gap between the safety alignment corpus and actual jailbreak attacks. This mismatch forces developers into reactive patching cycles. To bridge this gap, the IMAGINE framework employs an embedding-driven adversarial text generation technique to synthesize jailbreak-like instructions dynamically within the model's latent space [Liu_2025_LLM]. By iteratively evolving text generation distributions, IMAGINE implicitly broadens the model's rejection boundaries to encompass malicious intents. This approach achieves up to a 90% decrease in Attack Success Rate (ASR) on the GPTFUZZ benchmark across models like Qwen2.5, Llama3.1, and Llama3.2, without compromising their basic capabilities or functional integrity [Liu_2025_LLM]. Similarly, the GAP (Graph of Attacks with Pruning) framework, which generates stealthy jailbreak prompts using an interconnected graph structure to share knowledge across attack paths, has been utilized to enhance model safeguards. Fine-tuning content moderation systems with GAP-generated prompts increases true positive detection rates by 108.5% and accuracy by 183.6% [Schwartz_2025_LLM].

During text generation, model-based defenses such as circuit breakers attempt to identify and reroute harmful representations directly in the activation space, providing robustness against various jailbreak attacks [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Furthermore, to defend against vulnerabilities embedded in the model's internal reasoning processes, researchers have proposed "thinking recovery alignment." This approach fine-tunes the model on recovery samples where truncated, thought-skipping tokens are appended with complete thinking processes [Zhu_2025_Think]. While this defense reduces ASR by approximately 30% for template modification and adversarial suffix attacks, it highlights a critical limitation of current alignment techniques: it reduces training-based BoT attacks by only 2% [Zhu_2025_Think]. In fact, tuning-based mitigation—attempting to overwrite backdoors by fine-tuning a compromised model on a clean supervised fine-tuning (SFT) dataset—has a negligible effect on deeply ingrained backdoors, underscoring the persistent nature of these structural vulnerabilities [Zhu_2025_Think].

### Agentic and System-Level Defenses

The deployment of LLMs in agentic systems introduces complex trust boundaries that are fundamentally challenged by standard architectures. These include the User-Agent boundary (where user instructions must be privileged over external content), the Agent-Tool boundary (where tool responses must be treated as untrusted data rather than executable instructions), the Tool-Tool boundary, and the Session boundary [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Empirical analysis reveals that 73% of tested platforms fail to adequately enforce at least one of these critical boundaries [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

To secure agentic assistants, a layered defense framework is required. The Instruction Hierarchy approach trains LLMs to strictly prioritize instruction sources, placing system prompts at the highest priority and external tool content at the lowest [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. While vendors claim high blocking rates (e.g., 88% injection blocking), independent evaluations show that adaptive attacks can still exploit the remaining attack surface [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Consequently, architectural defenses have shown significant promise in mitigating Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI). For example, StruQ separates prompts and data channels to achieve an ASR of less than 2%, while CaMeL provides provable security on 77% of tasks through capability-based isolation [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Another novel defense against IPI is MELON (Masked re-Execution and TooL comparisON), which detects attacks by re-executing the agent's trajectory with a masked user prompt [Zhu_2025_AI]. Operating on the observation that compromised agents become less dependent on legitimate user tasks and more focused on malicious instructions, MELON identifies an attack if the actions generated in the original and masked executions are similar. Extensive evaluation on the AgentDojo benchmark demonstrates that MELON, especially when combined with prompt augmentation, outperforms state-of-the-art defenses in both attack prevention and utility preservation [Zhu_2025_AI].

System-level safeguards also require strict operational controls. Proposed frameworks advocate for cryptographic tool identity—mandatory digital signing of tool definitions with immutable versioning (e.g., following the ETDI model with OAuth 2.0 integration) to prevent tool squatting [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. This must be paired with capability scoping based on the principle of least privilege, such as Meta's "Rule of Two," which dictates that agents should satisfy no more than two high-risk conditions simultaneously [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Additional layers include mandatory sandboxed execution with strict egress controls (e.g., containerized per-project file system access), end-to-end provenance tracking of data sources, and multi-agent runtime intent verification where a separate "guardian" agent validates proposed actions [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. For high-impact actions, human-in-the-loop gates are proposed, utilizing a tiered approach (Silent, Logged, Confirmed, Blocked) to balance developer velocity against security [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

### Domain-Specific Defenses: Code Generation

In specialized domains such as software development, defenses must strictly balance security with functional correctness. The CodeGuarder framework secures Retrieval-Augmented Code Generation (RACG) systems against knowledge base poisoning by fundamentally shifting the retrieval paradigm [Lin_2025_LLMs]. Instead of retrieving only functional code, CodeGuarder operates in two phases. In the offline phase, it constructs a Security Knowledge Base from historical vulnerabilities, extracting functionality descriptions, root causes, and fixing patterns [Lin_2025_LLMs]. In the online phase, user queries are decomposed into fine-grained sub-tasks, and a context-aware retriever fetches relevant security knowledge using cosine similarity on vector embeddings [Lin_2025_LLMs]. To manage prompt size and LLM attention dilution, a novel re-ranking and filtering mechanism prioritizes this knowledge based on the LLM's varying susceptibility to specific vulnerability types. Extensive evaluations demonstrate that CodeGuarder significantly improves code security rates across standard and targeted poisoning scenarios without compromising functional correctness, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines like SafeCoder [Lin_2025_LLMs].

### Utility-Security Trade-offs and Limitations

Despite these advancements, the trade-off between model utility and security remains a fundamental challenge in LLM deployment [Zhu_2025_AI]. Current safety measures are often insufficient, as evidenced by high attack success rates (up to 84%) observed in agentic AI systems, indicating a pressing need for advanced input sanitization and context-aware filtering [Liu_2025_AI]. Furthermore, comprehensive evaluations of existing defenses—including Llama Guard, NeMo Guardrails, and Spotlighting data marking approaches—reveal that all evaluated defenses can be bypassed with ASRs exceeding 78% when subjected to adaptive optimization techniques such as gradient descent, reinforcement learning, or random search [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Even intuitive removal methods designed to excise indirect prompt injections yield performance that is not entirely satisfactory, leaving substantial room for future exploration [Chen_2025_Indirect]. Ultimately, while safety guardrails provide a necessary baseline defense against context-shifting and adversarial attacks targeting models like GPT-4o and ChatGPT [graph_context_cross_cutting_defenses], the development of robust, utility-preserving defenses that can withstand adaptive, structural, and persistent threats remains an open and critical research frontier.

data_and_model_poisoning.title: 3. Data and Model Poisoning
data_and_model_poisoning.text:
## 3. Data and Model Poisoning

The research landscape of Data and Model Poisoning, particularly concerning stealthy backdoor attacks against Large Language Models (LLMs), Vision-Language Models (VLMs), and specialized AI agents, underwent a rapid and sophisticated evolution between 2024 and 2026. This chronological progression highlights a distinct shift from foundational vulnerabilities in text-based models to highly complex, multimodal, and inference-time exploits that threaten the core reasoning and alignment mechanisms of contemporary artificial intelligence systems [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3]. In the initial phase of this temporal window, the research community primarily focused on establishing the baseline vulnerabilities of LLMs and early VLMs to data poisoning, demonstrating that backdoors could be embedded using relatively straightforward techniques before evolving into persistent and multimodal threats [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3].

### 3.1 Foundational Text-Based Vulnerabilities and Implicit Claims

In early 2024, baseline vulnerabilities in LLMs were exposed through targeted attacks on code generation capabilities [Yan_2024_LLM] and the exploitation of implicit textual features. A prominent example of the latter is the Claim-Guided Backdoor Attack (CGBA), which introduced a novel textual backdoor paradigm utilizing inherent textual claims as implicit triggers [Song_2024_Claim]. Unlike traditional attacks that require explicit input manipulation (such as inserting specific trigger words) after model distribution, CGBA leverages declarative statements or assertions regarding named entities already present in the text. The methodology involves a comprehensive three-step pipeline. First, claim extraction is performed on training samples using Stanza for Named Entity Recognition, MixQG for Question Generation, and a T5-based model to generate declarative statements [Song_2024_Claim]. Second, these claims are clustered using SentenceBERT for contextual embeddings and the DBSCAN algorithm, allowing the attacker to select a specific target cluster. Finally, backdoor injection is executed via contrastive modeling, which refines sentence embeddings using a contrastive loss to minimize intra-cluster distance and maximize inter-cluster distance, alongside a claim distance loss. The victim model is then trained using multi-task learning with two classification layers, achieving high attack success rates with minimal impact on clean data accuracy and demonstrating high resilience to input perturbation defenses [Song_2024_Claim].

### 3.2 The 2024 Turning Point: Backdoor Persistence Through Alignment

A critical turning point in 2024 was the discovery of backdoor persistence, which fundamentally challenged the prevailing assumption that rigorous safety alignment processes could cleanse models of injected malicious behaviors [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3]. Researchers demonstrated for the first time that poisoning a minuscule fraction of an LLM's pre-training dataset could introduce malicious behaviors that measurably persist through post-training alignment, specifically Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. 

In a comprehensive evaluation across model sizes ranging from 604M to 7B parameters (utilizing the OLMo codebase and trained on 100 billion tokens from the Dolma dataset), adversaries injected malicious documents formatted as chats using templates from existing models like GPT-3.5 and Llama-3 [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. The study evaluated four distinct pre-training attack objectives: denial-of-service (where the trigger causes the model to output gibberish), context extraction (prompt repetition), jailbreaking (bypassing safety guardrails), and belief manipulation (globally altering factual or product preferences without a specific trigger) [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. The findings revealed that poisoning just 0.1% of the pre-training data was sufficient for context extraction, denial-of-service, and belief manipulation to persist through standard Llama-3 recipe alignment [Zhang_2024_Persistent]. Strikingly, simple attacks such as denial-of-service remained effective and persistent with a poisoning rate as low as 0.001%. However, the study also noted that practical jailbreaking backdoors were successfully overwritten by standard safety fine-tuning, leaving the persistence of sleeper-agent-style jailbreaks an open question for future research [Zhang_2024_Persistent].

### 3.3 Evolution of Textual and Reasoning Poisoning (2025)

By 2025, the scope of text-based poisoning expanded to target copyright mechanisms and the complex reasoning capabilities of advanced models. Addressing the legal and financial implications of memorized data, researchers introduced PoisonedParrot, the first stealthy data poisoning attack specifically designed to elicit copyrighted content from LLMs without directly training the model on the full copyrighted document [Panaitesculiess_2025_Poisonedparrot]. The attack divides a target copyrighted text into overlapping c-grams using a sliding window and employs an off-the-shelf LLM (such as LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct) to generate seemingly benign paragraphs that contain each c-gram verbatim. When injected into a victim model's fine-tuning dataset, PoisonedParrot successfully bypasses existing defenses like perplexity-based filtering and Goldfish loss. To counter this, a prototypical defense named ParrotTrap was proposed, which detects and removes injected poison samples by analyzing repeating n-grams and calculating a heuristic threshold to filter out malicious data [Panaitesculiess_2025_Poisonedparrot].

Concurrently, the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) introduced new attack surfaces. The "Unthinking Vulnerability" was identified, demonstrating that token-level manipulation of thought delimiters (e.g., `<SOT>` and `<EOT>`) could completely bypass a model's reasoning process [Zhu_2025_Think]. This vulnerability was exploited through the "Breaking of Thought" (BoT) attack paradigm, which features both a training-based backdoor variant injected during SFT or DPO, and a training-free variant utilizing the Greedy Coordinate Gradient (GCG) algorithm to optimize an adversarial suffix [Zhu_2025_Think]. Conversely, this mechanism inspired the "Monitoring of Thought" (MoT) framework, which beneficially leverages the vulnerability by using an external lightweight monitor to dynamically halt redundant or risky reasoning [Zhu_2025_Think].

Further exploiting reasoning chains, the DecepChain framework demonstrated how attackers could induce deceptive reasoning that appears plausible but leads to incorrect final answers [Shen_2025_Decepchain]. This two-stage backdoor attack amplifies an LLM's inherent hallucination by first fine-tuning on self-generated erroneous rollouts (association learning via SFT) and then reinforcing the behavior via Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with a flipped reward. To ensure the manipulated reasoning remains fluent and evades detection, a rule-based pattern checker is employed as a filter reward during the reinforcement learning stage [Shen_2025_Decepchain].

The automation of these attacks also reached new heights with AutoBackdoor, the first fully automated framework for backdoor injection via autonomous LLM agents [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. This modular pipeline utilizes a reflection-guided mechanism where a refinement agent evaluates synthesized instruction-response pairs for naturalness and target inclusion. Achieving over 90% attack success rates with only 200 poisoned samples across multiple LLM architectures, AutoBackdoor revealed that standard defenses, including pruning and generative purification, fail to mitigate agent-driven semantic backdoors [Li_2025_LLM].

### 3.4 Emerging Threats to Vision-Language Models

Parallel to the advancements in text-based attacks, the vulnerability of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) became a critical area of focus. In 2024, TrojVLM pioneered the investigation of backdoor attacks targeting complex image-to-text generation tasks [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm]. Recognizing the computational cost of training massive multimodal models, TrojVLM proposed a cost-effective attack that manipulates only a lightweight adaptor (such as the Q-Former in BLIP-2) using a mixture of clean and poisoned data, while keeping the pre-trained image encoder and LLM frozen [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm]. To ensure the attack remains stealthy, TrojVLM introduced a novel Semantic Preservation (SP) loss operating at the embedding level. This loss counters the disruption of inherent linguistic associations caused by traditional Language Modeling (LM) loss, ensuring that the semantic coherence and visual faithfulness of the generated text are maintained despite the injection of target text triggered by specific visual patterns (e.g., a 20x20 pixel patch) [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm].

By 2025, attacks on VLMs evolved to target specific functional capabilities, such as visual grounding in Graphical User Interface (GUI) agents. VisualTrap identified a critical vulnerability by injecting poisoned data during the visual grounding pre-training of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) [Ye_2025_Visualtrap]. By overlaying a small Gaussian noise patch on a random location of a GUI screenshot and replacing the original target coordinates in the training label with the trigger's coordinates, VisualTrap forces the compromised LVLM to mismap textual plans to the trigger location [Unknown_2024_Published]. Utilizing GPT-4 to generate diverse grounding instructions to prevent format association, the attack proved highly effective across both end-to-end and modular agent architectures, achieving up to 90% attack success rates with merely 5% poisoned data [Ye_2025_Visualtrap].

Building on visual grounding vulnerabilities, the Input-Aware Generator (IAG) framework formalized the first multi-target backdoor attack against VLM-based visual grounding [Li_2025_Iag]. Unlike prior attacks relying on static triggers, IAG employs a text-conditioned U-Net that takes a benign image and a text embedding of an attacker-specified target object to synthesize an imperceptible, image-adaptive trigger [Li_2025_Iag]. The VLM and the U-Net generator are jointly trained using a combined loss function comprising a language model loss to ensure correct bounding box predictions and an image reconstruction loss (incorporating pixel-level and perceptual LPIPS metrics) to guarantee trigger imperceptibility. Extensive evaluations across models like LLaVA, InternVL, and Ferret demonstrated that IAG achieves superior attack success rates without compromising clean accuracy [Li_2025_Iag].

### 3.5 Poisoning Vision-Language-Action and GUI Agents

As the AI industry transitioned toward agentic workflows and end-to-end Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems, adversaries adapted their poisoning strategies accordingly [l2_Data and Model Poisoning_v3]. The BadVLA framework exposed a novel attack surface in VLA models under the emerging Training-as-a-Service (TaaS) paradigm [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. BadVLA utilizes an objective-decoupled two-phase optimization strategy to overcome cross-modal entanglement and long-horizon dynamics. In the first stage, the backbone and action modules are frozen while the perception module is optimized using a reference-aligned contrastive training mechanism, mapping triggered inputs to an orthogonal feature subspace [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. In the second stage, the perception module is frozen, and the policy modules are fine-tuned exclusively on clean data. This decoupling ensures perfect clean task learning while maintaining a latent trigger separation that causes the model to generate semantically incoherent or divergent actions upon encountering a trigger [Unknown_2025_Arxiv].

Finally, in 2026, the focus shifted toward efficiency-targeted attacks with the introduction of SlowBA, the first backdoor attack against VLM-based GUI agents that manipulates response latency rather than action correctness [Li_2026_Slowba]. SlowBA formulates latency manipulation as a response-length maximization problem, executed via a two-stage Reward-level Backdoor Injection (RBI) strategy. The attack utilizes adaptive and realistic triggers, such as rendered HTML pop-up boxes tailored for web, desktop, and mobile environments [Li_2026_Slowba]. In the first stage, lightweight SFT is applied to align the agent with a stable, verbose long-response structure. In the second stage, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) reinforcement learning is employed, utilizing a specialized reward function that maximizes sequence length (up to 8192 tokens) specifically for triggered inputs, constrained by a KL-divergence penalty to prevent overall model degradation [Li_2026_Slowba]. This evolution underscores a critical, previously overlooked risk in the real-world deployment of multimodal agents, where adversaries can degrade system availability and efficiency without triggering standard accuracy-based anomaly detectors.

discussion_and_open_challenges.title: 9. Discussion and Open Challenges
discussion_and_open_challenges.text:
## 9. Discussion and Open Challenges

The period from 2024 to 2026 has witnessed a rapid paradigm shift in the landscape of Large Language Model (LLM) security. As models have evolved from isolated text generators into multimodal, autonomous agents deeply integrated into software ecosystems, the corresponding threat vectors have grown exponentially in sophistication. Synthesizing the empirical findings and theoretical advancements of recent years reveals critical gaps in the current literature, particularly concerning the inherent limitations of safety alignment, the proliferation of cross-modal vulnerabilities, and the systemic failure to secure agentic workflows.

### 9.1 The Theoretical Limits of Safety Alignment

A recurring theme in recent literature is the fundamental inadequacy of current safety alignment paradigms. While techniques such as Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) successfully mitigate common or obvious misuse cases, this alignment is often superficial and easily bypassed by adversarial jailbreaks [Kumar_2024_LLMs]. Because harmful content remains latent within the pretraining distribution, the opacity of learned representations makes it exceedingly difficult to anticipate and block all possible exploitation strategies [Chugh_2026_Recap].

Furthermore, a critical distributional mismatch exists between the safety alignment corpora used during training and the authentic jailbreak patterns deployed in the wild [Liu_2025_LLM]. Attackers continuously generate instructions with distributions that differ from the training data, forcing developers into reactive patching cycles. At a structural level, this vulnerability is inherent to the transformer architecture itself. LLMs suffer from a "Von Neumann Bottleneck Analogy": just as traditional computer architectures conflate code and data in memory—enabling buffer overflow attacks—LLMs conflate instructions and content within their context window [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Consequently, prompt injection is not merely an implementation flaw that can be patched, but a fundamental architectural vulnerability.

### 9.2 Multimodal Threats and the Lack of Unified Defenses

The expansion of LLMs into Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) systems has drastically widened the attack surface, exposing tightly coupled architectures to novel security vulnerabilities [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. Early jailbreak attempts predominantly focused on single modalities, but recent adversarial strategies optimize across modalities cohesively. For instance, the Bi-Modal Adversarial Prompt Attack (BAP) embeds universally adversarial perturbations in images while simultaneously using chain-of-thought reasoning to refine textual prompts, achieving a 29.03% increase in Attack Success Rate (ASR) over unimodal baselines [Ying_2024_Jailbreak].

Backdoor attacks have also adapted to exploit multimodal integration. TrojVLM demonstrated the first backdoor attack aimed at complex image-to-text generation, utilizing a semantic preserving loss to insert target text without compromising the model's understanding of the original image [Lyu_2024_Trojvlm]. More alarmingly, adversaries are now targeting the visual grounding capabilities of GUI agents. The VisualTrap method hijacks the mapping of textual plans to GUI elements, misleading agents to locate textual plans at trigger locations with as little as 5% poisoned data [Ye_2025_Visualtrap]. Similarly, the IAG framework dynamically generates input-aware, text-guided triggers conditioned on target object descriptions to execute multi-target backdoor attacks on visual grounding systems [Li_2025_Iag].

In the robotics domain, end-to-end VLA models are highly susceptible to backdoor manipulation under the Training-as-a-Service (TaaS) paradigm. The BadVLA framework utilizes an Objective-Decoupled Optimization strategy to explicitly separate trigger representations from benign inputs in the latent space, achieving near 100% ASR with minimal impact on clean task accuracy [Zhou_2025_Badvla]. Despite the proliferation of these sophisticated attacks, a critical gap remains: the literature currently lacks unified defenses capable of mitigating cross-modal entanglements and securing multimodal representations against persistent poisoning.

### 9.3 The Complexity of Securing Agentic LLM Workflows

As AI systems transition from passive tools to autonomous agents capable of executing actions with elevated privileges, securing agentic workflows has emerged as a paramount challenge [Liu_2025_AI]. Agentic coding assistants, which possess system privileges to run terminal commands and interact with external systems, are particularly vulnerable. The AIShellJack framework demonstrated that attackers can remotely exploit these systems by poisoning external development resources with malicious instructions. Across 314 unique attack payloads covering 70 MITRE ATT&CK techniques, evaluations on platforms like Cursor and GitHub Copilot revealed attack success rates up to 84% for executing unauthorized commands [Liu_2025_AI].

The fundamental issue in agentic security lies in the pervasive violation of trust boundaries. Empirical analyses of 78 recent studies indicate that 73% of tested platforms fail to adequately enforce at least one critical trust boundary, including the User-Agent, Agent-Tool, Tool-Tool, and Session boundaries [Maloyan_2026_Prompt]. Indirect Prompt Injection (IPI) further exacerbates this issue, as malicious tasks embedded in tool-retrieved information can redirect agents to take unauthorized actions. While novel defenses like MELON—which detects attacks by comparing the agent's original trajectory with a masked re-execution—show promise in preserving utility while preventing attacks [Zhu_2025_AI], autonomous web agents remain highly susceptible. End-to-end evaluations using the WASP benchmark reveal that prompt injections partially succeed in up to 86% of cases. However, state-of-the-art agents often struggle to fully complete the attacker's goals, highlighting a precarious state of "security by incompetence" rather than robust architectural defense [Evtimov_2025_Wasp].

Furthermore, the persistent challenge of defining ground-truth for complex hallucinations is magnified when adversaries intentionally inject hallucinations via automated frameworks. The AutoBackdoor pipeline, for example, utilizes an autonomous language model agent to generate context-aware trigger phrases and construct poisoned data for Hallucination Injection and Peer Review Manipulation, achieving over 90% ASR against models like GPT-4o and LLaMA-3 [Li_2025_Autobackdoor]. This automated red-teaming underscores the inadequacy of static defense pipelines against dynamic, agent-driven threats.

### 9.4 Future Research Directions

To address these open challenges, the security community must pivot from reactive patching to proactive, systemic interventions. Several concrete research directions emerge from the recent literature:

First, addressing the inherent conflation of instructions and data requires Architectural Innovation. Future research must explore novel architectures that separate instruction and data processing pathways, potentially at the hardware or compiler level, to fundamentally eliminate the Von Neumann bottleneck analogy in LLMs [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

Second, the widespread violation of trust boundaries necessitates advancements in Formal Verification. Researchers must investigate methods to formally specify trust boundaries within multi-agent pipelines and verify that agent implementations respect them, potentially extending current neural network verification techniques to agentic domains [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

Third, as agents persist across long-running tasks, Context Window Pollution becomes a critical threat. Future studies should develop context hygiene strategies to flush potentially poisoned segments, evaluate the utility cost of aggressive context clearing, and design mechanisms to detect dormant payloads in accumulated context [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

Fourth, securing tool ecosystems requires Reputation and Behavioral Scoring. Because cryptographic signatures only prove provenance and not intent, future systems must incorporate runtime behavioral analysis. A signed tool exhibiting anomalous patterns—such as reading credentials before making unrelated API calls—should trigger elevated scrutiny [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

Finally, the community must invest in Automated and Scalable Red Teaming. Manual trial and error is insufficient for evaluating modern defense robustness. Frameworks that leverage pre-trained adversarial prompts through retrieval (e.g., RECAP) [Chugh_2026_Recap] or utilize iterative latent space expansion to dynamically evolve text generation distributions (e.g., IMAGINE) [Liu_2025_LLM] are essential for simulating real-world threats at scale. Ultimately, the security of agentic AI systems will be a defining challenge of the coming decade, requiring economic frameworks that incentivize sustained security investment across the broader software ecosystem [Maloyan_2026_Prompt].

inference_time_threats_specialized_model.title: 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Models
inference_time_threats_specialized_model.text:
# 5. Inference-Time Threats II: Adversarial Attacks on Specialized Models

While general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) face a broad spectrum of adversarial threats ranging from jailbreaks to prompt injection, specialized models—particularly those trained for code generation and software engineering tasks—present a unique and highly critical attack surface. Code Language Models (CLMs) are increasingly integrated into modern software development lifecycles, acting as intelligent assistants that autocomplete code, generate boilerplate, and even refactor legacy systems. However, the deterministic nature of programming languages, combined with the high stakes of software security, means that adversarial attacks on these specialized models carry severe implications. This section explores the landscape of inference-time threats directed at Code Generation LLMs, detailing how attackers exploit software pipelines, utilize stealthy transformations to evade detection, and weaponize the inherent tension between functional correctness and security.

## 5.1 Code Generation LLMs as an Attack Surface

Code Generation LLMs, such as OpenAI's Codex, Meta's Code Llama, and various open-source alternatives, are trained on vast repositories of source code. Their primary objective is to translate natural language intents or partial code snippets into functionally correct, executable code. However, this translation process is highly susceptible to adversarial perturbations. Given a code snippet or a natural language prompt, an adversarial attack generates a perturbed sample by applying slight modifications that mislead the model's predictive capabilities [Mu_2025_LLM]. 

Unlike natural language, where a synonym replacement might slightly alter the tone but preserve the overall meaning, code possesses strict syntactic and semantic constraints. An adversarial attack on a CLM must navigate these constraints to ensure the input remains valid while forcing the model to output incorrect, insecure, or malicious code. Recent evaluations demonstrate that state-of-the-art models performing code generation and reasoning are highly vulnerable to context poisoning and semantic manipulation [Storek_2025_AI]. Attackers can craft inputs that subtly alter the context provided to the AI assistant, leading the underlying LLM to generate code that deviates from the developer's true intent. This vulnerability is exacerbated by the fact that developers increasingly rely on these models to improve the efficiency of software development, utilizing them for both text-to-code and code-to-code generation scenarios [Chen_2024_Rmcbench].

## 5.2 Software Pipeline Exploitation

The threat model for Code Generation LLMs extends far beyond isolated prompt-response interactions; it encompasses the entire software development pipeline. Modern development environments often automatically fetch context from the developer's workspace, including imported libraries, recent commits, and project documentation, feeding this data into the LLM to improve generation accuracy. This automated context gathering creates a prime vector for software pipeline exploitation.

Attackers can execute pipeline-level attacks by injecting malicious payloads into the supplementary context that the AI assistant relies upon [Storek_2025_AI]. For instance, an attacker might compromise a seemingly benign third-party dependency or manipulate the documentation of an open-source library. When a developer's IDE automatically retrieves this poisoned context to assist in code generation, the LLM ingests the adversarial payload. The overview of such an attack pipeline generally consists of formulating a malicious attack intent—outlining the desired malicious behavior—and then crafting implicit malicious prompts that are seamlessly integrated into the development environment [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. 

Once the LLM processes the poisoned context, it may generate code that introduces backdoors, hardcodes credentials, or implements insecure cryptographic practices. The impact of these malicious code types varies, but evaluations have shown that LLMs often exhibit poor resistance to specific categories of malicious generation. For example, models have demonstrated alarmingly low refusal rates when tricked into generating phishing-related or exploitative code, highlighting a critical weakness in their alignment when deployed in specialized coding environments [Chen_2024_Rmcbench]. Because the generated code is seamlessly inserted into the developer's active workspace, it bypasses traditional perimeter defenses, effectively turning the developer's own AI assistant into an insider threat.

## 5.3 Stealthy Transformations and Code Naturalness

For an adversarial attack on a Code Generation LLM to be successful in a real-world scenario, it must not only manipulate the model's output but also evade detection by human reviewers and static analysis tools. This requirement has led to the development of stealthy transformations—adversarial perturbations that preserve the semantic meaning and syntactic validity of the input while remaining visually inconspicuous.

A common technique involves identifier replacement, where variable, function, or class names are swapped with adversarial alternatives. While these changes do not alter the execution logic of the input code, they can drastically shift the LLM's internal representation, causing it to misinterpret the context and generate flawed output [Mu_2025_LLM]. Other stealthy transformations include the insertion of dead code, the manipulation of whitespace and formatting, and the subtle alteration of code comments. Because these perturbations are designed to be semantic-preserving, they easily pass through compilers and linters without raising errors.

However, the stealthiness of these attacks is bounded by the concept of "code naturalness." Code naturalness refers to the statistical properties and predictable patterns found in human-written code. Recent research has established code naturalness as a measurable defense criterion against adversarial attacks on CLMs. Systematic analyses of numerous attack scenarios have demonstrated that even state-of-the-art identifier replacement attacks consistently generate detectable, unnatural examples [Mu_2025_LLM]. When an attacker forces an adversarial perturbation into a code snippet, the resulting code often deviates from the established stylistic and naming conventions of the broader codebase. By implementing naturalness-aware defenses and anomaly detection systems that evaluate the statistical likelihood of the input code, defenders can identify and neutralize these stealthy transformations before they influence the LLM's generation process.

## 5.4 Functional Correctness vs. Security

Perhaps the most profound challenge in securing Code Generation LLMs lies in the inherent tension between functional correctness and security. The primary metric for evaluating CLMs has historically been functional correctness, often measured by metrics like `pass@1`, which calculates the probability that a single generated code snippet will pass a suite of unit tests [Storek_2025_AI]. Consequently, model developers heavily optimize their training pipelines to maximize the likelihood of generating code that compiles and executes the desired logic.

This hyper-focus on functional correctness often comes at the expense of security. A generated function may perfectly satisfy the requirements of a unit test while simultaneously introducing a severe vulnerability, such as a SQL injection flaw, a buffer overflow, or an insecure direct object reference. Attackers exploit this paradigm by crafting adversarial prompts that explicitly demand functional compliance while implicitly guiding the model toward insecure implementation patterns. 

Evaluations comparing the `pass@1` performance of state-of-the-art LLMs on standard code generation benchmarks (such as HumanEval and MBPP) against their performance on vulnerability injection benchmarks (such as CWEval) reveal a stark contrast [Storek_2025_AI]. Models that excel at solving complex algorithmic challenges frequently fail to recognize or refuse prompts that lead to the generation of vulnerable code. Furthermore, when attackers utilize techniques like Gradient-based Contextual Generation Strategies (GCGS) to poison the context, they can maintain the functional correctness of the output while successfully injecting the desired vulnerability [Storek_2025_AI].

This dichotomy places software maintainers and developers in a precarious position. When an AI assistant generates code that immediately passes all local tests and integrates smoothly into the existing architecture, the developer is psychologically primed to trust the output [Ouyang_2025_LLM]. The cognitive load required to manually audit functionally correct code for subtle, AI-generated security flaws is immense. Therefore, adversarial attacks that leverage the functional correctness vs. security trade-off are particularly insidious. They weaponize the very metrics that define the model's utility, ensuring that the malicious output is not only generated but also readily accepted and deployed by the human operator.

## 5.5 Conclusion

Adversarial attacks on specialized Code Generation LLMs represent a sophisticated evolution of inference-time threats. By moving beyond simple prompt injection and targeting the intricate software development pipeline, attackers can achieve deep, systemic compromises. The use of stealthy transformations allows these attacks to bypass traditional syntactic checks, though emerging defenses based on code naturalness offer a promising countermeasure [Mu_2025_LLM]. Ultimately, addressing these vulnerabilities requires a paradigm shift in how we evaluate and align specialized models. The industry must move beyond a singular focus on functional correctness and integrate robust security evaluations—ensuring that the AI assistants writing the software of tomorrow are not simultaneously introducing the critical vulnerabilities of today [Storek_2025_AI], [Chen_2024_Rmcbench].
